questions.q: In merge sort, which of the three divide-and-conquer steps does the real work?
questions.explain: Merge sort divides trivially by cutting at the middle. All the comparisons happen while merging. Quick sort is the opposite: its partition (divide) does the work and its combine step is empty.
options: Divide: choosing where to cut
Conquer: the base case
Combine: merging two sorted halves
All three do the same amount

questions.q: Quick sort's combine step does nothing. Why is nothing needed?
questions.explain: The partition puts the pivot in its final position and separates smaller from larger items. Sorting each side in place finishes the job; there is nothing to merge.
options: Because quick sort only works on numbers
After partitioning, everything left of the pivot is smaller and everything right is larger, so once both sides are sorted the whole range is sorted in place
Because the recursion returns new arrays that are concatenated
Because quick sort is not really divide and conquer

questions.q: You find the largest of n order totals by divide and conquer (largest of each half, then compare the two). How many comparisons does it make?
questions.explain: Every order except the winner must lose exactly one comparison, so any method needs n − 1. Dividing only pays when it lets you skip work or when the combine step does something clever.
options: About log₂ n
About n log₂ n
Exactly n − 1, the same as a simple loop
About n / 2

questions.q: Two orders share the largest amount. What does this print?
questions.explain: B is in the left half and D in the right half. When the two halves' winners tie, >= keeps the left one. Deciding ties on purpose makes the answer predictable.
options: B
D
E
A

questions.q: How many calls does this divide-and-conquer sum make for 8 items?
questions.explain: The recursion tree has 8 leaves (one per item) and 7 internal nodes (each joins two parts): 2n − 1 = 15 calls. The tree has constant work per node, so the total is O(n), matching a loop.

questions.q: Why do the divide-and-conquer functions in the lesson pass lo and hi indexes instead of items.slice(0, mid)?
questions.explain: A slice is a new array, built by copying. In binary search that turns O(log n) into O(n). Merge sort can afford slices only because it already does O(n) work per level.
options: Slices are not allowed in recursive functions
Slicing copies the elements, which can add O(n) work per level and change the algorithm's complexity
Indexes use less stack space per call than arrays
Slices return the elements in reverse order

questions.q: What is a recursion tree used for?
questions.explain: Each node carries the work done by one call, excluding its children. Summing each level and then the levels gives the total. For merge sort each level sums to n and there are log₂ n levels.
options: Storing the results of recursive calls so they are not recomputed
Adding up the cost of a recursive algorithm: one node per call, labelled with the work that call does itself, summed level by level
Replacing recursion with a loop
Detecting infinite recursion at run time

questions.q: Merge sort runs on 4,096 items. How many levels of merging are there, and how many items are merged on each level?
questions.explain: 4,096 = 212, so halving reaches single items after 12 levels. On every level the merges together cover all 4,096 items once. That is 12 × 4,096 = n log₂ n.
options: 4,096 levels, 12 items each
12 levels, 4,096 items each
12 levels, halving each time: 4,096, 2,048, 1,024, …
64 levels, 64 items each

questions.q: What does bottom-up merge sort (merge runs of width 1, then 2, 4, 8, …) gain over the recursive version?
questions.explain: It does the same merges as the recursion tree, just from the leaves upwards. It still needs a buffer for merging, and it makes about the same number of comparisons.
options: Fewer comparisons
Stability
No recursion or call stack at all, and a level-by-level structure that works for data on disk (external sorting)
O(1) extra memory

questions.q: Bottom-up merge sort on 10 items: which run widths does it merge?
questions.explain: After merging runs of width 8, one run of 16 would cover all 10 items, so the loop stops once width reaches 16. The last runs on a level can be shorter than the width: the length does not need to be a power of two.

questions.q: While counting inversions during a merge, the item at right[j] is smaller than left[i] and is taken. How many inversions does that add?
questions.explain: The left half is sorted, so if right[j] is smaller than left[i], it is smaller than all of left[i..]. Each of those came earlier in the input and is larger: one inversion each.
options: j
left.length - i: it is smaller than every item still waiting in the left half
right.length - j

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The pairs in the wrong order are (2, 1), (4, 1) and (4, 3). A brute-force double loop gives the same answer in O(n²); the merge-based count is O(n log n).

questions.q: Quickselect uses the same partition as quick sort. Why is it O(n) on average while quick sort is O(n log n)?
questions.explain: Quick sort must sort both sides, so every level of its recursion tree does n work. Quickselect's recursion is a single path whose ranges shrink geometrically, and a geometric series is bounded by a constant times its first term.
options: It uses a faster partition
It continues into only the side that contains position k, so the work is about n + n/2 + n/4 + …, which is less than 2n
It stops after log n partitions
It sorts only the first k items

questions.q: Using the nearest-rank definition, which 0-based index k holds the 95th percentile of 200 values?
questions.explain: Nearest rank: position ⌈0.95 × 200⌉ = 190, counting from 1. Array indexes count from 0, so k = 190 - 1 = 189. Getting this wrong does not throw; it silently reports a neighbouring value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Sorted: 15, 20, 35, 40, 50. p40 is position ⌈2⌉ = 2 → 20. p50 is position ⌈2.5⌉ = 3 → 35. p90 is position ⌈4.5⌉ = 5 → 50.

questions.q: A two-way quickselect needs about 5 comparisons per item on distinct numbers, but almost 50 per item on 200,000 delivery times rounded to whole minutes. Why?
questions.explain: With many duplicates, the two-way partition behaves like quick sort on sorted data. A three-way partition (smaller, equal, larger) stops as soon as k falls among the equal items.
options: Rounded numbers are slower to compare
The random pivot is less random on rounded data
Thousands of deliveries share the same minute; a two-way partition sends all items equal to the pivot to one side, so ranges of equal items shrink by one per round
The median of rounded data is harder to find than the median of distinct data

questions.q: This is one three-way partition around the pivot 3. What does it print?
questions.explain: Smaller items end up in a[0..lt-1], equal ones in a[lt..gt] and larger ones in a[gt+1..]. If the k you want is between 2 and 4, the answer is 3 and you can stop. The smaller and larger parts are not guaranteed to be sorted in general; here they happen to be.
options: 1 2 3 3 3 4 5 | equal from 2 to 4
1 2 3 3 3 5 4 | equal from 2 to 4
2 1 3 3 3 4 5 | equal from 2 to 4
1 2 3 3 3 4 5 | equal from 3 to 5

questions.q: Why is n + n/2 + n/4 + n/8 + … less than 2n however many terms you add?
questions.explain: n/2 + n/4 + n/8 + … approaches n but never reaches it. This geometric sum is why quickselect is O(n) and why the "root wins" case of the master theorem costs O(f(n)).
options: Because the series stops after log n terms
Each term is half the previous one, so the terms after n add up to less than n: every time you add a term, you cover half of the remaining gap to 2n
Because n/2 + n/4 is always less than n/2
It is not; it grows like n log n

questions.q: The quickselect in the lesson starts with const a = [...input]. What would go wrong without the copy?
questions.explain: Partitioning swaps items around. The copy costs O(n) memory and time, which does not change quickselect's O(n) complexity, and it keeps the function free of side effects. If memory is tight, reorder in place and document it clearly.
options: The function would return the wrong value
It would be O(n²)
It would reorder the caller's array, surprising any other code (a chart, another percentile) that uses it
Nothing; partitioning does not move items

questions.q: A quickselect always uses the last item of the range as the pivot. What is its cost on an array that is already sorted, when you ask for the smallest item (k = 0)?
questions.explain: The last item is the largest, so each partition removes only that one item and continues with n − 1, n − 2, … items: about n²/2 comparisons. A random pivot avoids depending on the input order.
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n²)

questions.q: This quickselect partitions the caller's array in place. What does the last line print?
questions.explain: The pivot 30 lands at index 2 after one partition, so the answer is found immediately. But the partition rearranged the caller's minutes array, which now reads 10 20 30 40 50. Any code that relied on the original order (for example, the order deliveries happened in) is now wrong.

questions.q: Which identity lets you compute x<sup>n</sup> with about log₂ n multiplications?
questions.explain: Each step halves the exponent at the cost of one squaring, plus one extra multiplication when the exponent is odd. The first identity is the slow loop: n − 1 multiplications.
options: x<sup>n</sup> = x × x<sup>n − 1</sup>
x<sup>n</sup> = (x<sup>n/2</sup>)² for even n, and x × (x<sup>(n − 1)/2</sup>)² for odd n
x<sup>n</sup> = x<sup>n/2</sup> + x<sup>n/2</sup>
x<sup>n</sup> = n × x

questions.q: How many multiplications does this fast power make for exponents 8 and 7?
questions.explain: Exponent 8 recurses through 4, 2, 1 and 0: four squarings, plus one extra multiplication at the odd exponent 1. Exponent 7 goes through 3, 1, 0: three squarings plus one extra at each odd exponent (7, 3, 1). The total is between log₂ n and 2 log₂ n, plus one.

questions.q: Why does powMod apply % modulus after every multiplication instead of only at the end?
questions.explain: 51,000,003 has about 700,000 digits. Reducing after each step keeps the numbers small and every multiplication cheap, and the remainder rule guarantees the same final answer.
options: Because JavaScript requires it for BigInt
Because (a × b) mod m equals ((a mod m) × (b mod m)) mod m, so reducing early gives the same answer while keeping every number below m²
To make the result negative-safe
It makes no difference to speed or memory

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A regular number cannot represent 253 + 1, so it rounds to 253. BigInt is exact at any size, which is why modular power works with BigInt. 1024 mod 1000 is 24.

questions.q: Merge sort follows T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. Which master theorem case is it, and why?
questions.explain: Compare f(n) with nlogb a = nlog₂ 2 = n. They grow alike, so each of the log n levels contributes n: Θ(n log n).
options: Leaves win, because there are n leaves
Tie: f(n) = n grows like n<sup>log₂ 2</sup> = n, so every level does the same work and the cost is n × log n
Root wins, because the root merges all n items
The master theorem does not apply to merge sort

questions.q: An algorithm multiplies two n-digit numbers by splitting each in half and computing four half-size products, then adding them in O(n): T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n. What is its cost?
questions.explain: nlog₂ 4 = n², which grows faster than f(n) = n, so the leaves win: Θ(n²). Karatsuba's trick of needing only three products gives nlog₂ 3 ≈ n1.585.
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(n²)
O(n⁴)

questions.q: Quickselect's average case is T(n) = T(n/2) + n. What does the master theorem give, and which part of the tree dominates?
questions.explain: With a = 1 there is one leaf, and the work per level halves as you go down: n + n/2 + … < 2n. The root's own work decides the total.
options: Θ(n log n); every level does n work
Θ(n); the root dominates, because n<sup>log₂ 1</sup> = 1 grows more slowly than f(n) = n
Θ(log n); the leaves dominate
Θ(n²); the leaves dominate

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 is the divide-and-conquer maximum: 2n − 1 nodes in its recursion tree, each costing 1. The leaves win (nlog₂ 2 = n beats f(n) = 1), so it is Θ(n).

questions.q: For a recurrence where the leaves dominate, which change makes the biggest difference to the cost?
questions.explain: When leaves win, f(n) does not appear in the answer at all. Karatsuba reduced a from 4 to 3 and the exponent from 2 to about 1.585. When the root wins, it is the other way round: make f(n) cheaper.
options: Making the combine step f(n) cheaper
Reducing the number of subproblems a (or making them smaller), because the cost is n<sup>log<sub>b</sub> a</sup>
Using iteration instead of recursion
Choosing a random pivot

questions.q: Quick sort with a bad pivot on sorted data has T(n) = T(n − 1) + n. How do you find its cost?
questions.explain: The master theorem needs subproblems of size n/b with b > 1. When in doubt, draw the tree and sum the levels: n + (n − 1) + … + 1 = n(n + 1)/2.
options: Master theorem with a = 1, b = 1
The master theorem does not apply (the size shrinks by subtraction, not division); draw the recursion tree: a path of n levels doing n, n − 1, … work, about n²/2
It is O(n log n) like every quick sort
It is O(n) because a = 1

questions.q: This binary search slices the array on every step. What does it print?
questions.explain: The halves copied are 4, then 2, then 1 item(s): 7 in total, about n. The comparisons are O(log n), but the copying makes the whole search O(n). Passing lo and hi indexes avoids every copy.
options: false 7
false 3
false 0
false 8

questions.q: This search rounds the midpoint up and keeps [lo, mid]. A safety counter stops it after 10 rounds. What does it print?
questions.explain: For the range [0, 1], Math.ceil(0.5) is 1, so hi = mid leaves the range unchanged: the subproblem never shrinks. Without the counter it would loop forever (or overflow the stack in a recursive version). Round down when you keep [lo, mid], and test ranges of one and two items.

questions.q: "Ways to pay ₦n with ₦50 and ₦100 notes" splits into ways(n − 50) + ways(n − 100). Solving the two parts independently takes exponential time. Why, and what is the fix?
questions.explain: Divide and conquer assumes independent parts, like the two halves of merge sort. When parts share sub-subproblems, solve each distinct subproblem once and store it: that is dynamic programming.
options: The split is unbalanced; use a random split
The subproblems overlap (both need ways(n − 150), and so on), so the same work is repeated exponentially often; remember each answer (dynamic programming)
The recursion is too deep; use a loop
The combine step is too expensive; use a heap

questions.q: A monitoring system must report p95 latency over billions of requests from 50 servers every minute. Why is quickselect not the right tool?
questions.explain: Quickselect is exact but needs the full data set. Sketches trade a small, known error for tiny memory and the ability to combine summaries from many servers.
options: Quickselect cannot find percentiles above p50
It needs all values in memory in one place; such systems use mergeable sketches (such as HDR histograms or t-digest) that answer percentile queries approximately from small summaries
Quickselect is O(n²) on latency data
Percentiles must be exact, and quickselect is approximate

questions.q: Real merge sort and quick sort implementations stop dividing at around 16 to 64 items and finish those pieces with insertion sort. Why?
questions.explain: Big O describes growth for large n. For 20 items, an O(n²) algorithm with a tiny constant beats an O(n log n) one with call overhead. Hybrid algorithms use each where it is best.
options: Insertion sort has a better Big O
For tiny inputs the overhead of recursive calls outweighs the n log n advantage, and insertion sort is very fast on small or nearly sorted pieces
Merge sort cannot sort fewer than 16 items
To make the sort stable

questions.q: Which property of a divide-and-conquer algorithm makes it easy to run on several cores or machines?
questions.explain: The two halves of merge sort share nothing until the merge, so they can be sorted in parallel. That is the idea behind map-reduce and parallel query engines, and it only pays when the combine step is cheap.
options: It uses recursion
It has a base case
Its subproblems are independent, so they can be solved at the same time and combined afterwards
It is always O(n log n)

questions.q: Write power(base, exponent) for whole-number exponents by squaring (no **, no Math.pow, no loop of exponent multiplications). It should print 1024 59049 1 1.1025.
questions.explain: The base case is exponent 0. Each call halves the exponent, so there are about log₂ n calls, each doing one or two multiplications. Store the half power in a variable: writing power(b, e/2) * power(b, e/2) makes two calls per level and turns O(log n) back into O(n).

questions.q: Write kthSmallest(values, k) (k counted from 0) with quickselect: partition around a pivot into smaller, equal and larger items, and continue only into the part that contains position k. Do not sort the whole array. It should print 35 15 90 20.
questions.explain: This version partitions with filter into new arrays: simpler than in-place swapping, and it never changes the caller's array, at the cost of extra memory. When k falls into the right part, subtract the sizes of the parts you skipped. The "equal" part handles duplicates in one step. With a middle pivot, some inputs still make it quadratic; the lesson's version uses a random pivot.

questions.q: Last month's ranks of this month's top products are listed in this month's order. Count the flipped pairs (inversions) in O(n log n) by counting during merge sort. It should print 0 1 4 10.
questions.explain: Inversions inside each half are counted by the recursive calls; inversions between the halves are counted during the merge, left.length - i at a time. For [3, 1, 4, 5, 2] the flipped pairs are (3,1), (3,2), (4,2) and (5,2).

questions.q: Write mergeAll(lists) that merges any number of sorted lists of order ids by divide and conquer: merge the first half of the lists, the second half, then merge the two results. It should print 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9, then an empty line for no lists, then 4 5.
questions.explain: Two base cases: no lists (nothing to merge) and one list (already merged). Each item takes part in about log₂ k merges, so the total is O(N log k). Slicing the list of lists is cheap here: it copies k references, not the orders.

questions.q: Write percentile(values, p) using the nearest-rank definition (sorting is fine here). Throw a RangeError for an empty array and for p outside (0, 100]. It should print 20 50 no values p must be above 0 and at most 100.
questions.explain: p25 of 5 values is position ⌈1.25⌉ = 2, which is 20; p95 is position ⌈4.75⌉ = 5, which is 50. Writing the check as !(p > 0 && p <= 100) also rejects NaN, because every comparison with NaN is false.
questions.expected: 20 50 no values p must be above 0 and at most 100

questions.q: Write sortBottomUp(values): merge runs of width 1, then 2, 4, … with no recursion. It should print 3 9 10 27 38 43 82, then 5, then an empty line.
questions.explain: Math.min clips the last runs at the end of the array, so any length works, including 0 and 1 (the loop never runs). Each width is one level of the merge sort recursion tree, done from the bottom up.

questions.q: Fibonacci numbers can be computed with fast power: the matrix [[1, 1], [1, 0]] raised to the power n contains F(n) in its top-right corner. Write multiply(a, b) for 2×2 matrices and matrixPower(m, n) by squaring, then fib(n). It should print 0 1 55 12586269025.
questions.explain: Fast power works for anything with an associative multiplication. The base case is the identity matrix (the matrix version of 1). fib(50) needs about 6 levels instead of 50 steps. Beyond fib(78) the numbers exceed 253, so a real version would use BigInt.
